newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Mandela gives S.African navy hope of new ships.
newsitem.headline: Mandela gives S.African navy hope of new ships.

text.p: President Nelson Mandela gave South African navy chiefs hope on Saturday that they would get new craft to replace a fleet which is kept afloat with scrap-heap pickings.
"The need to modernise our fleet is not a matter of debate," Mandela said in a speech at an international naval parade to mark the 75th anniversary of the South African navy.
"I expect that the defence review will herald the renaissance of the South African navy, the maritime shield of the nation and the guardian of our seas," Mandela said.

A parliamentary committee is due to complete its review of South Africa's defence needs within weeks, and Defence Minister Joe Modise intends to tell parliament of his spending plans by the end of May.
Modise has been trying for more than two years to buy four corvettes, but parliament froze negotiations with foreign companies at an advanced stage pending the defence review.

Bazan shipyards of Spain had been the favoured supplier but Deputy Defence Minister Ronnie Kasrils said on Friday that Britain had since made "interesting" proposals for the supply of corvettes and submarines. He said the tendering process would be reopened.
South Africa's four Daphne-class submarines are nearly 30 years old and at the end of their useful lives. The country is picking through scrapyards in Europe for spares for the vessels.

"Changing priorities have led to a reduction in the defence budget," Mandela said on Saturday. "But we do recognise our responsibility for ensuring that our country has an adequate and appropriate naval force."

Modise, who was at Mandela's side for the naval parade on Saturday, said this week that members of parliament appeared to have accepted the need to upgrade the navy. South Africa has nine relatively small surface strike craft in the 400-tonne range to patrol 3,000 km (1,900 miles) of coastline.
Ships from about 30 countries, including Russia, Britain and the United States, took part in the naval parade.
They sailed in through Table Bay between Robben Island and Cape Town harbour as Mandela, who was jailed on the island for 18 years, took the salute from a South African navy ship.
